top_news.title: Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image Renovated Dakar Railway station inaugurated, May 2026. 2026 Human Rights Watch Senegal's intensifying crackdown on LGBT people is violating their rights and causing increasing fear and stigma.Fear of arrest and stigma are causing people to go into hiding, to avoid HIV testing and treatment, and deterring lawyers from representing them.The crackdown on LGBT people calls into question Senegal's compliance with its own laws and international law, as well as the Olympic charter, given it will host the Youth Olympics Games at the end of the month. (Dakar) Senegal's growing crackdown on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) people is violating their rights, causing increasing fear and stigma, and should be ended immediately, Human Rights Watch said today. Mass arrests forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation appear to be part of an increase in punitive government action against LGBT people inWest Africa. On March 11, 2026, Senegal's parliament amended article 319 ofthe penal code, doubling to 10 years the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and criminalizing "promotion" of or support to LGBT people and organizations. The amendment followed the detention by security forces of at least five men in This region in December 2025 and12 men in the capital, Dakar, in February 2026 on charges including "acts against nature" and "intentional transmission of HIV." Police and gendarmerie then escalated arrests of suspected LGBT people in various other cities includingThis,Rosso,Saint Louis, Yeumbeul, andZiguinchor. "LGBT people are being forced to curb their normal activities and to keep from exercising their rights for fear of arrest and increased stigma," saidLarissa Kojoue, LGBT rights researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Senegal's government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone's rights." Human Rights Watch interviewed 39 people in May in Senegal: 5 people who had been detained in late 2025 and early 2026, 2 journalists, 9 civil society representatives and human rights defenders, 2 national officials, 2 lawyers, 4 health professionals, and 15 members of the Senegalese queer community. Human Rights Watch also reviewed official statements, and media and nongovernmental group reports. On September 29, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Senegalese authorities, including the justice minister, the high commander of the National Gendarmerie and director of military justice, and the director general of the National Police detailing its findings and asking specific questions, but has received no response. Same-sex sexual conducthas been criminalized in Senegal since 1965, but hostility toward LGBT people has significantlyintensified in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Diomaye Faye and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonkopledged to strengthen laws criminalizing same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority and mobilizing broad political and public support. The March amendments have triggered new attacks against LGBT people, interviewees said. Mouhamadou Seck, secretary-general of the prominent Senegalese organization African Forum for the Defense of Human Rights (Rencontre Africaine pour la Defense des Droits de l'Homme, or RADDHO), said in May that "detentions, violence, and abuse against LGBT individuals have sharply increased across the country." Human Rights Watch was not able to independently verify the total number of arrests linked to article 319. However, between February and July, at least 212 people have been arrested, according to data collected by RADDHO. HIV Justice Networkreported that the number of arrests exceeded more than 300 during the same period. Of those arrested, 82 were alsocharged with "voluntary HIV transmission," although a court dismissed these charges in August. These figures illustrate the scale of arrests and indicate a pattern in enforcement of article 319. Security force officials havestated that they have arrested people suspected of engaging in same-sex conduct based on information extracted from previously seized phones, third-party allegations, or raids on private premises. TheMarch amendment to the penal code introduces broadly defined offenses criminalizing activities such as "promotion" and "glorification" of homosexuality, as well as financing and supporting LGBT individuals and organizations. Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of these offenses has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation. "In Senegal, lawyers are associated with the cause they represent," a lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch, adding that his colleagues and family members had urged him not to represent individuals arrested on charges of "acts against nature." He said: "Everyone has the right to a fair trial. What matters to me is: were their rights respected or not?" Principle 18 of the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provides that "Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients' causes as a result of discharging their functions." People interviewed said that since February, the authorities have subjected detainees to HIV testing without informed consent and used detainees' HIV status to justify additional criminal charges or prolonged detention. Health professionals expressedconcern that the forced HIV testing and subsequent charges undermine medical confidentiality by allowing confidential test results to be used in criminal proceedings. They also discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment and jeopardize HIV-related public health efforts. "We have noticed that [...] some people have fled while others are hiding," a doctor in Dakar said. "One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment." Security forces also appear to have violated the confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBT people.News reporting on two cases involving public figures includes personal details that closely track details set forth in investigative records, suggesting authorities leaked confidential information to journalists. Local media also extensivelyreported personal and confidential data on the case of the 12 men arrested in February. This has exposed individuals tosocial stigma, family rejection, threats, and violence. TheSenegalese Constitution and international human rights law applicable in Senegal guarantee fundamental rights, including equal protection before the law and non-discrimination; the right to effective legal representation and the presumption of innocence; the rights to privacy and to informed consent to medical treatment; freedom from torture and other ill-treatment, and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. Senegal'sLaw No. 2010-03 of April 9, 2010, on HIV/AIDS establishes a legal framework to ensure access to treatment and support and protect the rights of people living with or affected by HIV. The law guarantees the rights to informed consent in medical testing and to privacy and confidentiality of health information, as well as protection against discrimination based on HIV status and protection of detainees from mandatory HIV testing. The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, ratified by Senegal in 1982, guarantees, among other rights, the right to a fair trial, to equal protection before the law, and to nondiscrimination. The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, which will meet in Dakar from October 12-21, explicitly called on member states, including Senegal, to protect sexual minorities in accordance with the African charter, and has urged governments to protect people from violence based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Senegal is a party, requires Senegal to ensure the protection of numerous rights including fair trial, equal protection, nondiscrimination, and the right to privacy. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, has repeatedly held that the criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct between adults violates the covenant. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will host theDakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event on the African continent. TheOlympic Charter prohibits discrimination on any grounds and commits host countries to respect human rights and human dignity. "The ongoing government crackdown on LGBT people raises serious concerns about Senegal's compliance with international law, the Olympic charter, and Senegal's own laws," Kojoue said. "The government should call a halt to this crackdown." Click to expand Image Interview with Sall (pseudonym), university student in Dakar, Senegal, who has barely left his room since February due to stigma and fear of arrest, May 2026. 2026 Human Rights Watch Expanded Criminalization of Same-Sex Conduct On March 11, Senegal's Parliament adoptedamendments to article 319 of the penal code by a vote of 135 to 0, with three abstentions. The new law doubles, to 10 years, the maximum prison term for same-sex conductand increases fines from 2 million to 10 million CFA francs (roughly US$3,000 to US$17,000). The law introduces penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5 million CFA ($850 to $8,500) for those accused of promoting homosexuality or supporting or financing LGBT persons and organizations. It also instructs judges not to suspend sentences or reduce prison terms below the minimum penalty recommended. Arbitrary Arrest, Detention According todata from July by the HIV Justice Network, since early February, authorities "have arrested over 300 individuals on allegations of acts against nature" in cities across Senegal. Data collected by RADDHO shows 212 people were arrested between February and July. RADDHO told Human Rights Watch that their data indicates that gendarmes from the Keur Massar unit carried out the majority of the arrests. Keur Massar is about 25 kilometers east of downtown Dakar. On June 25, Keur Massar district gendarmerie arrested the101st suspect in connection with the arrest wave that began in February, according to media reports. Officers said the arrests followed their review of a mobile phone seized from one of the 12 men arrested in February. In July 30,international media reported that Keur Massar gendarmes arrested eight women who have been placed in pretrial detention. The gendarmes used phone data from two who were allegedly in a relationship to identify and arrest the six others. Beside "acts against nature," investigators also cited allegations of pimping, corruption of minors, and drug-related offenses. Police in the This region, about 70 km east of Dakar, arrested five men in December 2025 for smoking shisha, a tobacco product banned under local law, and held them for two days before presenting them to a judicial authority. The prosecutor ordered them held on charges of "acts against nature" but dropped the charges and released them a month later for lack of evidence. They said that they believe neighbors denounced them to the authorities because of their sexual orientation. One of the five, a 23-year-old man, said: We were arrested while preparing for a fashion show at my place. Around 9 p.m., three police officers arrived, took us to the station and confiscated our phones.... We were held for two days, then taken to the This prosecutor's office and charged with acts against nature, despite not being caught in the act.... I think our neighbors told the police we are gay because they were jealous of our successful fashion business. He said that, "we were beaten, whipped, and slapped, and called homosexuals.... I was injured on my thigh, causing lasting pain." A social worker operating in Rebeuss, Senegal's largest detention facility, located in Dakar, said he witnessed prison staff and detainees discriminate against those held on suspicion of homosexuality: "[LGBT detainees] are being excluded from communal activities, denied participation in collective prayer sessions, and required to access services, including the barber, separately from other prisoners. In some cases, they are even compelled to perform domestic labor." Prolonged Pretrial Detention Since February, only one person arrested for "acts against nature" has been convicted according tolocal media. On April 10, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court, in a suburb of Dakar, sentenced a 24-year-old man, who had been arrested a week earlier, to six years in prison and imposed a fine of 2 million CFA franc (approximately $3,300) after convicting him of "acts against nature" and "public indecency." He was not represented by legal counsel as it is often the case for people accused of "acts against nature" who may be denied access to legal representation or face difficulty finding lawyers willing to represent them. A lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch that many of those arrested on homosexuality-related charges remain in pretrial detention because prosecutors have added supplementary charges, including criminal association, endangering the life of others, deliberate HIV transmission, and drug trafficking. The lawyer said that these additional charges often require longer investigations and are used to justify extending pretrial detention. Senegalese law generally limits pretrial detention to six months for minor offenses, with no limit for certain serious crimes such as murder, offenses against state security, and embezzlement of public funds.International human rights law requires that pretrial detention should be an exception, not the rule, and be justified on an individual basis in every case. Anyone held in pretrial detention is entitled to a trial within a reasonable time or release. Lengthy pretrial detention remains a significant concern in Senegal, as several civil society organizations and government officials interviewed said. On August 7, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court officiallyclosed the preliminary investigation into the case involving the 12 men arrested on February 9 and another 87 people arrested in connection with the same crackdown. The court dismissed cases for 28 and freed them, but 71 remain referred to trial on charges of criminal association and acts against nature. The district court also dismissed charges of "endangering other people's lives" and "voluntary HIV transmission." This decision raises questions regarding continued detention of the 12 accused as the investigative needs that are commonly invoked to justify prolonged pretrial detention may no longer apply. Barriers to Legal Representation Human Rights Watch found that that the newly introduced offense of "promotion of homosexuality" has had a chilling effect on access to legal representation. Lawyers and human rights defenders said they were concerned that representing people charged under article 319 could expose them to professional, social, or even legal repercussions. "How can we represent people arrested without being accused of promotion," one lawyer said. "That's why there is such strong reluctance." The lawyer described serious obstacles to accessing legal representation, saying that detainees, including his own client, were pressured to waive their right to legal representation. He also said that authorities frequently questioned detainees and obtained statements in the absence of legal counsel. On February 9, the lawyer filed two complaints before the Dakar Court of Appeals, one on his own behalf and one on behalf of his client against a gendarmerie commander who pressured his client to waive his right to legal representation. He said in September that no progress had been made in either case. Another lawyer raised concern about gendarmes' respect for due process. He suspected that authorities had obtained his clients "confessions" without their fully understanding of the proceedings and the implications of their statements. Forced HIV Testing; Disclosure of Medical Information RADDHO and HIV Justice Network told Human Rights Watch that the authorities have forced most detainees to undergo HIV testing and, when the results were positive, charged them with "deliberate HIV transmission" and "endangering the lives of others" in addition to offenses under article 319 of the amended penal code. Under article 36 of Senegal's 2010law on HIV/AIDS, anyone who is knowingly living with HIV and has unprotected sex may face 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine. The Keur Massar gendarmerie hasofficially stated that they required arrested people to undergo HIV tests. The national police also have conducted such tests and used the HIV status in criminal proceedings, as they mentioned in their June 13statement. "We are aware about nonconsensual HIV testing by gendarmerie and disclosure of people's HIV status," a doctor told Human Rights Watch. The consequences of these practices have extended beyond individual detainees. Health professionals said that the use of HIV-related services has sharply declined and attribute it to fear of arrest, forced disclosure, and social stigma. "If, because of the law, people decide to stop coming to health clinics, it becomes a public health problem," a doctor said. The Public Health Ministry and the National Council for the Fight Against AIDS (Conseil National de Lutte Contre le Sida, or CNLS), a government body leading and coordinating the HIV response in Senegal, released joint statements on Facebook onFebruary 11 andFebruary 23 stressing national efforts to treat and prevent HIV/AIDS and support people living with HIV/AIDS, as well as the need to keep medical and judicial records separate, and the difficulty of establishing intentional transmission. In a March 18 news statement, the Joint UN Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), which advocates for global action against the HIV/AIDS pandemic, expressed concerns over the impact of the amended law, andcalled on Senegal to protect the confidentiality of medical information and the patient-provider relationship as non-negotiable foundations of a functioning health system. Breaches of Privacy and Confidentiality Numerous local media reports on the recent cases include highly detailed personal information about individuals arrested by the security forces. In at least four cases, the information closely tracks information in case records, nearly verbatim, suggesting that confidential information was being directly shared with journalists. "Our photos and items found [by Police] at my home, like lubricants and antiretroviral tablets, were published in newspapers and on social media," the 23-year-old man said. In one prominent case, a rare instance in which the detainee had legal representation after his arrest, Keur Massar gendarmes detained a popular artist on charges of "acts against nature," and his name, HIV status, and other confidential information appeared soon afterward in themedia. As a Senegalese journalist put it: "Publishing 'scandalous' information, on such a taboo matter like homosexuality in Senegal, has increasingly become a means of driving audience engagement. This practice turns people's suffering into spectacle, with little regard for the serious consequences for those whose privacy and dignity are violated." Mental Health Consequences of the Crackdown The government crackdown has had serious social and psychological effects on LGBT people across the country. LGBT individuals interviewed said they experienced fear, anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts, and many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements, withdrawn from social and online life, relocated, or abandoned mobile phones to avoid detection by the security forces. A 22-year-old university student said he was forced to move after facing verbal threats and harassment: In the neighborhood where I was, people started insulting me. They would say things like 'next time it is your turn,' when I passed [by them]. Kids would even follow me singing 'goor-jigeen' [a Wolof word describing a man who appears and behaves like a woman] and adults would say nothing. I couldn't even defend myself. I knew if I said something, they would all come after me. To come back home I had to wait until it is dark so no one would notice me. A 27-year-old community worker in Dakar, said constant fear has turned daily life "into a state resembling COVID confinement": We have suspended all our activities, including online. Now nobody trusts anyone. There is a total lack of security. I know I have one foot in prison. I can be arrested anytime because I am a community leader. Even if I am not in prison right now, I live like I am in prison. Life has totally changed. Another 21-year-old man among those arrested in December 2025 said that, following his release in January 2026, he has been living in hiding in central Senegal, unable to return home out of fear his relatives would assault him: I received a call from my mother telling me not to come back home. Apparently, my [half] brothers and some of my cousins were waiting for me and [were] ready to teach me a lesson. I have been hiding since. I couldn't even go back home to pick up some stuff. I have withdrawn from several online groups and deactivated my social media. Many of my friends left for Gambia, Mauritania, or Morrocco. I am staying because I am my mother's only child. A 35-year-old man in Ziguinchor said his partner left with no prior notice for a neighboring country causing him psychological distress: My partner left the country at night on a motorbike when he heard that his close friends were arrested and the police raided his place. He threw away his phone. He lives in poor conditions on the other side of the border. He does not have his medication. I am scared for him. A psychologist at Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar said that her consultations on campus "have tripled" since March. "Many patients are young men experiencing severe anxiety, hypervigilance, withdrawal from social life, and obsessive behaviors driven by fear of being perceived and attacked as LGBT." Recommendations To Senegal's President Order the immediate release of everyone arbitrarily detained since February 2026 under article 319 of the penal code.Refer the amended law to the Constitutional Council for constitutional review of its compatibility with constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy, equality before the law, non-discrimination, and fair trial rights.Publicly commit, ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, to ensure that all participants, visitors, and residents alike, will be protected from discrimination and arbitrary arrests. To the National Assembly Repeal article 319 in its entirety, including the provisions of the amended penal code that criminalize the "promotion" or "glorification" of homosexuality, as well as the financing or support of LGBT individuals and organizations.Initiate a legislative review to remove HIV status as a criminal aggravating factor. To Senegal's Government Open an investigation of abuses documented against LGBT people and hold those responsible accountable.Instruct judicial authorities to uphold national and international laws to guarantee access to legal representation for all detainees and ensure lawyers can represent clients without intimidation, harassment, or risk of prosecution.Ensure that pretrial detention is an exceptional measure, not a standard procedure, and that anyone in such detention is guaranteed a trial within a reasonable time or release.Prohibit forced HIV testing, ensure informed consent for all medical testing, prevent the use of confidential health information in criminal proceedings, and protect medical confidentiality, including by prohibiting the disclosure of detainees' health information to the media.Open an independent investigation into the case concerning a gendarmerie commander who pressured a detainee to waive his right to legal representation before leaking the detainee's HIV status to journalists.Respect and protect the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly, including for individuals and organizations advocating for the rights of LGBT people. To the National Medical Council Reaffirm that forced HIV testing violates medical ethics.

They said that they believe neighbors denounced them to the authorities because of their sexual orientation. One of the five, a 23-year-old man, said: We were arrested while preparing for a fashion show at my place. Around 9 p.m., three police officers arrived, took us to the station and confiscated our phones.... We were held for two days, then taken to the This prosecutor's office and charged with acts against nature, despite not being caught in the act.... I think our neighbors told the police we are gay because they were jealous of our successful fashion business. He said that, "we were beaten, whipped, and slapped, and called homosexuals.... I was injured on my thigh, causing lasting pain." A social worker operating in Rebeuss, Senegal's largest detention facility, located in Dakar, said he witnessed prison staff and detainees discriminate against those held on suspicion of homosexuality: "[LGBT detainees] are being excluded from communal activities, denied participation in collective prayer sessions, and required to access services, including the barber, separately from other prisoners. In some cases, they are even compelled to perform domestic labor." A lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch that many of those arrested on homosexuality-related charges remain in pretrial detention because prosecutors have added supplementary charges, including criminal association, endangering the life of others, deliberate HIV transmission, and drug trafficking. The lawyer said that these additional charges often require longer investigations and are used to justify extending pretrial detention. Senegalese law generally limits pretrial detention to six months for minor offenses, with no limit for certain serious crimes such as murder, offenses against state security, and embezzlement of public funds.International human rights law requires that pretrial detention should be an exception, not the rule, and be justified on an individual basis in every case. Anyone held in pretrial detention is entitled to a trial within a reasonable time or release. Lengthy pretrial detention remains a significant concern in Senegal, as several civil society organizations and government officials interviewed said. On August 7, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court officiallyclosed the preliminary investigation into the case involving the 12 men arrested on February 9 and another 87 people arrested in connection with the same crackdown. The court dismissed cases for 28 and freed them, but 71 remain referred to trial on charges of criminal association and acts against nature. The district court also dismissed charges of "endangering other people's lives" and "voluntary HIV transmission." Barriers to Legal Representation Human Rights Watch found that that the newly introduced offense of "promotion of homosexuality" has had a chilling effect on access to legal representation. Lawyers and human rights defenders said they were concerned that representing people charged under article 319 could expose them to professional, social, or even legal repercussions. "How can we represent people arrested without being accused of promotion," one lawyer said. "That's why there is such strong reluctance." The lawyer described serious obstacles to accessing legal representation, saying that detainees, including his own client, were pressured to waive their right to legal representation. He also said that authorities frequently questioned detainees and obtained statements in the absence of legal counsel. On February 9, the lawyer filed two complaints before the Dakar Court of Appeals, one on his own behalf and one on behalf of his client against a gendarmerie commander who pressured his client to waive his right to legal representation. Health professionals said that the use of HIV-related services has sharply declined and attribute it to fear of arrest, forced disclosure, and social stigma. In one prominent case, a rare instance in which the detainee had legal representation after his arrest, Keur Massar gendarmes detained a popular artist on charges of "acts against nature," and his name, HIV status, and other confidential information appeared soon afterward in themedia. They would say things like 'next time it is your turn,' when I passed [by them]. Kids would even follow me singing 'goor-jigeen' [a Wolof word describing a man who appears and behaves like a woman] and adults would say nothing. I couldn't even defend myself. I knew if I said something, they would all come after me. To come back home I had to wait until it is dark so no one would notice me. Apparently, my [half] brothers and some of my cousins were waiting for me and [were] ready to teach me a lesson. I have been hiding since. I couldn't even go back home to pick up some stuff. top_news.title: Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image Renovated Dakar Railway station inaugurated, May 2026. 2026 Human Rights Watch Senegal's intensifying crackdown on LGBT people is violating their rights and causing increasing fear and stigma.Fear of arrest and stigma are causing people to go into hiding, to avoid HIV testing and treatment, and deterring lawyers from representing them.The crackdown on LGBT people calls into question Senegal's compliance with its own laws and international law, as well as the Olympic charter, given it will host the Youth Olympics Games at the end of the month. (Dakar) Senegal's growing crackdown on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) people is violating their rights, causing increasing fear and stigma, and should be ended immediately, Human Rights Watch said today. Mass arrests forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation appear to be part of an increase in punitive government action against LGBT people inWest Africa. On March 11, 2026, Senegal's parliament amended article 319 ofthe penal code, doubling to 10 years the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and criminalizing "promotion" of or support to LGBT people and organizations. The amendment followed the detention by security forces of at least five men in This region in December 2025 and12 men in the capital, Dakar, in February 2026 on charges including "acts against nature" and "intentional transmission of HIV." Police and gendarmerie then escalated arrests of suspected LGBT people in various other cities includingThis,Rosso,Saint Louis, Yeumbeul, andZiguinchor. "LGBT people are being forced to curb their normal activities and to keep from exercising their rights for fear of arrest and increased stigma," saidLarissa Kojoue, LGBT rights researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Senegal's government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone's rights." Human Rights Watch interviewed 39 people in May in Senegal: 5 people who had been detained in late 2025 and early 2026, 2 journalists, 9 civil society representatives and human rights defenders, 2 national officials, 2 lawyers, 4 health professionals, and 15 members of the Senegalese queer community. Human Rights Watch also reviewed official statements, and media and nongovernmental group reports. On September 29, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Senegalese authorities, including the justice minister, the high commander of the National Gendarmerie and director of military justice, and the director general of the National Police detailing its findings and asking specific questions, but has received no response. Same-sex sexual conducthas been criminalized in Senegal since 1965, but hostility toward LGBT people has significantlyintensified in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Diomaye Faye and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonkopledged to strengthen laws criminalizing same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority and mobilizing broad political and public support. The March amendments have triggered new attacks against LGBT people, interviewees said. Mouhamadou Seck, secretary-general of the prominent Senegalese organization African Forum for the Defense of Human Rights (Rencontre Africaine pour la Defense des Droits de l'Homme, or RADDHO), said in May that "detentions, violence, and abuse against LGBT individuals have sharply increased across the country." Human Rights Watch was not able to independently verify the total number of arrests linked to article 319. However, between February and July, at least 212 people have been arrested, according to data collected by RADDHO. HIV Justice Networkreported that the number of arrests exceeded more than 300 during the same period. Of those arrested, 82 were alsocharged with "voluntary HIV transmission," although a court dismissed these charges in August. These figures illustrate the scale of arrests and indicate a pattern in enforcement of article 319. Security force officials havestated that they have arrested people suspected of engaging in same-sex conduct based on information extracted from previously seized phones, third-party allegations, or raids on private premises. TheMarch amendment to the penal code introduces broadly defined offenses criminalizing activities such as "promotion" and "glorification" of homosexuality, as well as financing and supporting LGBT individuals and organizations. Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of these offenses has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation. "In Senegal, lawyers are associated with the cause they represent," a lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch, adding that his colleagues and family members had urged him not to represent individuals arrested on charges of "acts against nature." He said: "Everyone has the right to a fair trial. What matters to me is: were their rights respected or not?" Principle 18 of the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provides that "Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients' causes as a result of discharging their functions." People interviewed said that since February, the authorities have subjected detainees to HIV testing without informed consent and used detainees' HIV status to justify additional criminal charges or prolonged detention. Health professionals expressedconcern that the forced HIV testing and subsequent charges undermine medical confidentiality by allowing confidential test results to be used in criminal proceedings. They also discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment and jeopardize HIV-related public health efforts. "We have noticed that [...] some people have fled while others are hiding," a doctor in Dakar said. "One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment." Security forces also appear to have violated the confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBT people.News reporting on two cases involving public figures includes personal details that closely track details set forth in investigative records, suggesting authorities leaked confidential information to journalists. Local media also extensivelyreported personal and confidential data on the case of the 12 men arrested in February. This has exposed individuals tosocial stigma, family rejection, threats, and violence. TheSenegalese Constitution and international human rights law applicable in Senegal guarantee fundamental rights, including equal protection before the law and non-discrimination; the right to effective legal representation and the presumption of innocence; the rights to privacy and to informed consent to medical treatment; freedom from torture and other ill-treatment, and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. Senegal'sLaw No. 2010-03 of April 9, 2010, on HIV/AIDS establishes a legal framework to ensure access to treatment and support and protect the rights of people living with or affected by HIV. The law guarantees the rights to informed consent in medical testing and to privacy and confidentiality of health information, as well as protection against discrimination based on HIV status and protection of detainees from mandatory HIV testing. The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, ratified by Senegal in 1982, guarantees, among other rights, the right to a fair trial, to equal protection before the law, and to nondiscrimination. The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, which will meet in Dakar from October 12-21, explicitly called on member states, including Senegal, to protect sexual minorities in accordance with the African charter, and has urged governments to protect people from violence based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Senegal is a party, requires Senegal to ensure the protection of numerous rights including fair trial, equal protection, nondiscrimination, and the right to privacy. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, has repeatedly held that the criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct between adults violates the covenant. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will host theDakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event on the African continent. top_news.title: Trkiye: End Internet Censorship
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image Tags, with "Access blocked" and the name of blocked accounts belonging to journalists and media outlets, LGBT and women's rights groups, and other rights defenders, are tied to the gates of Turkey's Constitutional Court, to protest the Turkish authorities' blocking of hundreds of social media accounts and websites. Ankara, October 7, 2026. 2026 Yldz Yazcolu (Istanbul, October 12, 2026) - The Turkish authorities over the last month have substantially escalated internet censorship, Human Rights Watch said today, along with ARTICLE 19, the Freedom of Expression Association, and 18 other organizations. Social media platforms should take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to suppressing independent media and violating the right to freedom of expression. The Turkish authorities should stop issuing blocking orders to restrict content and accounts on social media and websites in violation of the right to freedom of expression. The following is the groups' statement: ARTICLE 19, Freedom of Expression Association (FD), Human Rights Watch, and the undersigned human rights and media freedom organisations are deeply concerned by the severe escalation of internet censorship in Trkiye in the past month. We urge social media platforms to take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to the suppression of independent media and violations of the right to freedom of expression. We call on the Turkish government immediately to cease the use of blocking orders and other restrictive measures that violate the right to freedom of expression, and to ensure that any restrictions on online content fully comply with Trkiye's obligations under international human rights law. In the month of September 2026 alone,FD documented Turkish authorities and courts ordering the blocking of access to at least 1,270 accounts on the social media platform X, which had a combined following of 35 million. X complied with at least 90 percent of the orders by geo-blocking them (withholding access to them in Trkiye only). In many cases, the accounts were blocked in the context of an ongoing andwide-ranging crackdown on associations and activists defending the rights of LGBTQ+ people. In other cases, the authoritiescited unspecified "national security and public order" grounds. Accounts withheldinclude news outlets such as sold Haber and Mezopotamya Ajans; rights organisations including Amnesty Trkiye and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA); LGBTQ+; and women's rights organisations such as Kaos GL and the Federation of Women's Associations, as well as those of numerous journalists and academics. X alsowithheld the accounts of FD, its co-founder, Yaman Akdeniz, and its Engelliweb account, which monitors and documents internet censorship in Trkiye. This account plays a critical role in enabling civil society, journalists, and the public to monitor and track websites, social media accounts and content subjected to access restrictions. Blocking T24, one of Trkiye's biggest and oldest remaining independent news outlets, is particularly troubling. On 29 September,access was blocked to the T24 website and X account with 1.9 million followers, with a court order citing 118 news articles published on the site. The order claimed that the content was "aimed at disrupting and weakening the Turkish family structure" and of a nature "that would adversely affect the developmental process of young and underage individuals concerning sexual orientation and gender identity." The order cited preventing crime and protecting public order as grounds for the measure but provided no explanation about how the cited content posed a threat to either objective or why blocking an entire news website and social media account was necessary and proportionate. The website has been inaccessible in Trkiye since 30 September. T24 changed its X handle in an attempt to prevent the account from being withheld in Trkiye, then changed it again, after another order blocked access to its second handle. Bianet, another online news outlet which focuses on human rights, also changed its X handle to escape censorship after itsaccount with 400,000 followers was blocked. The court order blocking access to T24 was taken in the context of the "my family is safe" criminal investigations - a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people which targets activists, associations and a journalist advocating for their rights. The websites and social media accounts of at least 96 organizations and individuals wereblocked on the same grounds. While most of the cases concern X, Meta has alsowithheld access to the Instagram and Facebook accounts of several media and civil society organisations, including, Ksa Dalga, Kaos GL, and the Civic Space Studies Association as part of the same operation. Trkiye's long-standing abuse of Article 8/A of its Internet Law Most of the blocking decisions in September and October invoked Article 8/A of Trkiye's Internet Law. Article 8/A, used as a tool for internet censorship since its introduction in 2015, provides that online content deemed a threat to national security, public order or presenting a risk on other grounds listed in the article can be removed or blocked on orders of the executive in urgent cases, subject to review later by a Criminal Peace Judgeship, the court assigned such cases. Major examples include blocking access to Wikipedia for 2.5 years in 2017, and to Trkiye's leading user-generated online discussion platform Eki Szlk for a year in 2023. The Constitutional Court eventually restored both, finding that blocking the entire sites had violated freedom of expression. The use of Article 8/A intensified sharply from 2025, with few safeguards or independent oversight and limited redress for those affected. The Constitutional Court has not ruled on any restrictions under Article 8/A since 2023. Concerning developments aimed at expanding censorship There is no indication that this pressure will ease. On the contrary, the government is taking further measures to accelerate and centralise internet censorship. On 31 July, Law No. 7590 transferred the powers previously exercised by the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA) contained in the Internet Law, to the Cybersecurity Directorate. This includes the authority to block sites on the request of the presidency or relevant ministries based on Article 8/A. This transfer of authority istroubling. The Cybersecurity Directorate is directly attached to the presidency, consolidating executive control over information and serving as thecommand centre for Trkiye's censorship regime. Separately, on 24 September, the justice minister announced the establishment of new "Digital Space Security and Countering Disinformation Bureaux," where specialised public prosecutors will closely monitor "criminal content and activities encouraging crime on digital platforms" including 'spreading disinformation." They are tasked in particular with identifying suspects and initiating criminal proceedings to intervene "more swiftly." Social media platforms should take urgent action to uphold their human rights responsibilities The conduct of social media platforms forms an essential part of internet censorship in Trkiye. In September and early October, account holders reported receiving only a notification from platforms stating that their account had been withheld in Trkiye under Article 8/A, without any reason or explanation why or how the article had been applied. Some wereunable to access the underlying blocking orders even after repeatedly requesting them from the platforms. Without access to the orders, users cannot examine the legal basis for the restriction or even identify to which Criminal Judgeship of Peace to submit their objections. Even when users were able to obtain the orders, the orders often failed to identify the specific content allegedly justifying the blocking of the entire account. Neither X nor Meta have provided public explanations about their responses to the September-October censorship waves. Human Rights Watch wrote to the two platforms requesting comment on their compliance with Turkish courts' recent blocking orders. Neither platform had responded by the time of publication. Under the UNGuiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, companies have a responsibility to respect human rights by avoiding causing or contributing to adverse human rights impacts and by addressing impacts directly linked to their operations, products, or services. This responsibility should also inform social media platforms when they respond to government requests that violate international human rights law, and in particular freedom of expression. We therefore urge X, Meta, and any other platform faced with such orders by the Turkish government to also follow these recommendations: Resist complying with arbitrary 8/A requests Refuse to comply with account blocking requests under Article 8/A of the Internet Law unless Turkish authorities identify the specific content at issue and provide sufficient reasoning and evidence demonstrating that the content gives rise to a clear, serious and imminent danger to the right to life and property, national security and public order, public health or other ground listed in the provision.Where account blocking orders provide sufficient information to enable a meaningful assessment, assess them against international human rights law and resist complying with blocking orders that restrict access to protected expression. This includes but is not limited to legally challenging such orders. Where relevant, limit restrictions in scope and duration, for example by restricting access only to the specific content identified in the order rather than withholding the entire account. Ensure transparency Immediately notify users when their accounts are withheld in Trkiye and provide them with the orders on which the restriction is based. This allows account holders to take necessary steps to challenge the orders.Provide transparency concerning account blocking measures, at least by publicly sharing the number of orders received, the number of orders complied with, and publishing case studies. This information is essential for enabling public scrutiny of government censorship and platforms' role in it. Engage with Turkish civil society Meaningfully engage with Turkish civil society to understand the human rights implications and broader impact of platforms complying with account blocking measures, including the significance of the accounts targeted and the potential consequences of withholding them in Trkiye. Urgently review appeals to restrictions Review user appeals to account restrictions imposed in Trkiye in September and October 2026 and immediately restore access to accounts if the underlying orders fail to meet the requirements of identifying the specific content at issue, establishing a link between that content and the alleged threat to national security, public order and other grounds listed in Article 8/A, and providing adequate reasoning demonstrating that blocking the entire account is necessary and proportionate. We call on Turkish authorities to take urgent steps to end internet censorship and uphold freedom of expression, including by Immediately halting new restrictions on online content that violate freedom of expression, media freedom, and access to information as protected under international law and Trkiye's human rights obligations.Restoring access to content which has been restricted in violation of international law and Trkiye's freedom of expression obligations Signatories: ARTICLE 19Freedom of Expression Association (FD)Human Rights WatchAmnesty InternationalAssociation of European Journalists (AEJ)Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN)Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)ada Gazeteciler Dernei (GD, Progressive Journalists Association)Foreign Media Association (FMA Turkey)IFEXInternational Press Institute (IPI)Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA)Norwegian Helsinki Committee (NHC)Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)P24 Platform for Independent JournalismPEN AmericaPEN DenmarkPEN InternationalPEN NorwaySouth East Europe Media Organisation (SEEMO)Turkey Litigation Support Project (TLSP)

top_news.title: UN: Burundi Set to Win Human Rights Council Seat Despite Abuses
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image Burundi's President Evariste Ndayishimiye speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, in New York, New York, September 23, 2026. 2026 AP Photo/Heather Khalifa (New York) - Burundi is set to win re-election to the United Nations Human Rights Council in a vote on October 12, 2026, with no competition, Human Rights Watch said today. Burundi is seeking to retain its seat even though the government of this Central African country has not improved its abusive human rights conditions. Burundi is one of the four African countries running for the same number of seats on the 47-nation council. The regional slates for the Western group, Latin America and the Caribbean, Central and Eastern Europe, and Asia also lack competition. This effectively guarantees all 15 candidates, fit or unfit, spots on the UN's premier rights body for three years beginning on January 1, 2027. "This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word 'election,'" said Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch. "UN member states should insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records. No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter." Ghana, Nigeria, and Zambia are candidates for Africa's other three available seats. In Asia, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, and Nepal are running for the region's four seats. In Latin America and the Caribbean, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Uruguay are set to take the region's three spots. For the Western group, Germany and Ireland are on track to get the group's two available seats, while Moldova and Ukraine will take Central and Eastern Europe's two spots. Despite some positive government statements, Burundi has not carried out meaningful reform to address longstanding concerns related to governance, justice, or accountability. Grave abuses persist with impunity, including extrajudicial executions, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, and detention. Freedom of expression, assembly, and association remain severely restricted. Burundi is in the third year of its current term and is allowed to run for another consecutive term. On October 6, the country's delegation tried to use their membership to prevent UN scrutiny of Burundi's poor human rights record, first by calling a vote to renew the mandate of the UN special rapporteur on Burundi and then by voting against it. The resolution was adopted, though, 22 to 7, with 17 abstentions. That resolution not only expressed concerns about ongoing rights violations but highlighted Burundi's refusal to cooperate with the council and most of its mechanisms, including the special rapporteur. General AssemblyResolution 60/251, which created the Human Rights Council in 2006, says that countries voting for members should "take into account the contribution of candidates to the promotion and protection of human rights." Council members are required to "uphold the highest standards in the promotion and protection of human rights" at home and abroad and to "fully cooperate with the Council." Candidates only need a simple majority in the secret-ballot vote in the 193-nation General Assembly to secure a seat on the Human Rights Council. That makes it highly unlikely that any candidate will lose, no matter how unqualified. Nevertheless, UN member states should not cast votes for abusive governments that are demonstrably unqualified for council membership. Among the other candidates, Nigeria should ensure accountability for serious international crimes committed by all parties-including security forces-during the conflict with the armed group Boko Haram. Brazil should investigate and curb police abuse after law enforcement officers set a grim record in 2025 by killing more than 6,500 people, the vast majority of them Black. Ukraine has suffered countless atrocities committed by Russian forces on its territory since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. At the same time, Ukrainian authorities have unjustly prosecuted Ukrainian civilians living under Russian occupation, including teachers, medics, municipal workers, and volunteers for doing essential work that international humanitarian law permits civilians to perform under occupation. The Human Rights Council scrutinizes all UN member states' rights records in the Universal Periodic Review process. In November 2025, the United States refused to participate in its review. If the US government does not participate in its rescheduled review in November, it will become the first member country not to complete its review. The Human Rights Council has played a crucial role in ensuring independent investigations of abuses inSyria,Myanmar,North Korea, Russia, Ukraine, Israel/Palestine, Afghanistan, Sudan, and elsewhere. Council members should press for investigations of abuses by other countries in need of scrutiny, including major powers. These should includeChina's crimes against humanity against Uyghurs and others inXinjiang, as well as the US military's unlawful strikes targeting vessels the Caribbean and Pacific, amounting to extrajudicial killings. The council should also explore possible action to support global justice in the face of a US assault on international accountability mechanisms. The US on October 9 imposed unjustified sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump administration has made clear its aim to destroy the ICC to shield US and Israeli officials from facing charges before the court. The US had previously sanctioned ICC officials, Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian Territory occupied since 1967, and several prominent Palestinian human rights groups. "The human rights movement is under increasing attack by powerful governments, including established democracies," Charbonneau said. "The Human Rights Council has done victims of human rights abuses a huge service with investigations that often deter governments and armed groups from committing violations. We need the council now more than ever."

articles.title: Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People
articles.summary: Click to expand Image Renovated Dakar Railway station inaugurated, May 2026. 2026 Human Rights Watch Senegal's intensifying crackdown on LGBT people is violating their rights and causing increasing fear and stigma.Fear of arrest and stigma are causing people to go into hiding, to avoid HIV testing and treatment, and deterring lawyers from representing them.The crackdown on LGBT people calls into question Senegal's compliance with its own laws and international law, as well as the Olympic charter, given it will host the Youth Olympics Games at the end of the month. (Dakar) Senegal's growing crackdown on Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, and Transgender (LGBT) people is violating their rights, causing increasing fear and stigma, and should be ended immediately, Human Rights Watch said today. Mass arrests forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation appear to be part of an increase in punitive government action against LGBT people inWest Africa. On March 11, 2026, Senegal's parliament amended article 319 ofthe penal code, doubling to 10 years the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex conduct and criminalizing "promotion" of or support to LGBT people and organizations. The amendment followed the detention by security forces of at least five men in This region in December 2025 and12 men in the capital, Dakar, in February 2026 on charges including "acts against nature" and "intentional transmission of HIV." Police and gendarmerie then escalated arrests of suspected LGBT people in various other cities includingThis,Rosso,Saint Louis, Yeumbeul, andZiguinchor. "LGBT people are being forced to curb their normal activities and to keep from exercising their rights for fear of arrest and increased stigma," saidLarissa Kojoue, LGBT rights researcher at Human Rights Watch. "Senegal's government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone's rights." Human Rights Watch interviewed 39 people in May in Senegal: 5 people who had been detained in late 2025 and early 2026, 2 journalists, 9 civil society representatives and human rights defenders, 2 national officials, 2 lawyers, 4 health professionals, and 15 members of the Senegalese queer community. Human Rights Watch also reviewed official statements, and media and nongovernmental group reports. On September 29, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Senegalese authorities, including the justice minister, the high commander of the National Gendarmerie and director of military justice, and the director general of the National Police detailing its findings and asking specific questions, but has received no response. Same-sex sexual conducthas been criminalized in Senegal since 1965, but hostility toward LGBT people has significantlyintensified in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, President Diomaye Faye and former Prime Minister Ousmane Sonkopledged to strengthen laws criminalizing same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority and mobilizing broad political and public support. The March amendments have triggered new attacks against LGBT people, interviewees said. Mouhamadou Seck, secretary-general of the prominent Senegalese organization African Forum for the Defense of Human Rights (Rencontre Africaine pour la Defense des Droits de l'Homme, or RADDHO), said in May that "detentions, violence, and abuse against LGBT individuals have sharply increased across the country." Human Rights Watch was not able to independently verify the total number of arrests linked to article 319. However, between February and July, at least 212 people have been arrested, according to data collected by RADDHO. HIV Justice Networkreported that the number of arrests exceeded more than 300 during the same period. Of those arrested, 82 were alsocharged with "voluntary HIV transmission," although a court dismissed these charges in August. These figures illustrate the scale of arrests and indicate a pattern in enforcement of article 319. Security force officials havestated that they have arrested people suspected of engaging in same-sex conduct based on information extracted from previously seized phones, third-party allegations, or raids on private premises. TheMarch amendment to the penal code introduces broadly defined offenses criminalizing activities such as "promotion" and "glorification" of homosexuality, as well as financing and supporting LGBT individuals and organizations. Human rights defenders and lawyers said that the introduction of these offenses has led to fear and anxiety among legal professionals and contributed to an environment in which detainees struggle to secure legal representation. "In Senegal, lawyers are associated with the cause they represent," a lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch, adding that his colleagues and family members had urged him not to represent individuals arrested on charges of "acts against nature." He said: "Everyone has the right to a fair trial. What matters to me is: were their rights respected or not?" Principle 18 of the United Nations Basic Principles on the Role of Lawyers provides that "Lawyers shall not be identified with their clients or their clients' causes as a result of discharging their functions." People interviewed said that since February, the authorities have subjected detainees to HIV testing without informed consent and used detainees' HIV status to justify additional criminal charges or prolonged detention. Health professionals expressedconcern that the forced HIV testing and subsequent charges undermine medical confidentiality by allowing confidential test results to be used in criminal proceedings. They also discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment and jeopardize HIV-related public health efforts. "We have noticed that [...] some people have fled while others are hiding," a doctor in Dakar said. "One-third no longer come in for appointments to seek HIV treatment." Security forces also appear to have violated the confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBT people.News reporting on two cases involving public figures includes personal details that closely track details set forth in investigative records, suggesting authorities leaked confidential information to journalists. Local media also extensivelyreported personal and confidential data on the case of the 12 men arrested in February. This has exposed individuals tosocial stigma, family rejection, threats, and violence. TheSenegalese Constitution and international human rights law applicable in Senegal guarantee fundamental rights, including equal protection before the law and non-discrimination; the right to effective legal representation and the presumption of innocence; the rights to privacy and to informed consent to medical treatment; freedom from torture and other ill-treatment, and the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. Senegal'sLaw No. 2010-03 of April 9, 2010, on HIV/AIDS establishes a legal framework to ensure access to treatment and support and protect the rights of people living with or affected by HIV. The law guarantees the rights to informed consent in medical testing and to privacy and confidentiality of health information, as well as protection against discrimination based on HIV status and protection of detainees from mandatory HIV testing. The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, ratified by Senegal in 1982, guarantees, among other rights, the right to a fair trial, to equal protection before the law, and to nondiscrimination. The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, which will meet in Dakar from October 12-21, explicitly called on member states, including Senegal, to protect sexual minorities in accordance with the African charter, and has urged governments to protect people from violence based on their sexual orientation and gender identity. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Senegal is a party, requires Senegal to ensure the protection of numerous rights including fair trial, equal protection, nondiscrimination, and the right to privacy. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, has repeatedly held that the criminalization of consensual same-sex conduct between adults violates the covenant. From October 31 to November 13, Senegal will host theDakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympic event on the African continent. TheOlympic Charter prohibits discrimination on any grounds and commits host countries to respect human rights and human dignity. "The ongoing government crackdown on LGBT people raises serious concerns about Senegal's compliance with international law, the Olympic charter, and Senegal's own laws," Kojoue said. "The government should call a halt to this crackdown." Click to expand Image Interview with Sall (pseudonym), university student in Dakar, Senegal, who has barely left his room since February due to stigma and fear of arrest, May 2026. 2026 Human Rights Watch Expanded Criminalization of Same-Sex Conduct On March 11, Senegal's Parliament adoptedamendments to article 319 of the penal code by a vote of 135 to 0, with three abstentions. The new law doubles, to 10 years, the maximum prison term for same-sex conductand increases fines from 2 million to 10 million CFA francs (roughly US$3,000 to US$17,000). The law introduces penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5 million CFA ($850 to $8,500) for those accused of promoting homosexuality or supporting or financing LGBT persons and organizations. It also instructs judges not to suspend sentences or reduce prison terms below the minimum penalty recommended. Arbitrary Arrest, Detention According todata from July by the HIV Justice Network, since early February, authorities "have arrested over 300 individuals on allegations of acts against nature" in cities across Senegal. Data collected by RADDHO shows 212 people were arrested between February and July. RADDHO told Human Rights Watch that their data indicates that gendarmes from the Keur Massar unit carried out the majority of the arrests. Keur Massar is about 25 kilometers east of downtown Dakar. On June 25, Keur Massar district gendarmerie arrested the101st suspect in connection with the arrest wave that began in February, according to media reports. Officers said the arrests followed their review of a mobile phone seized from one of the 12 men arrested in February. In July 30,international media reported that Keur Massar gendarmes arrested eight women who have been placed in pretrial detention. The gendarmes used phone data from two who were allegedly in a relationship to identify and arrest the six others. Beside "acts against nature," investigators also cited allegations of pimping, corruption of minors, and drug-related offenses. Police in the This region, about 70 km east of Dakar, arrested five men in December 2025 for smoking shisha, a tobacco product banned under local law, and held them for two days before presenting them to a judicial authority. The prosecutor ordered them held on charges of "acts against nature" but dropped the charges and released them a month later for lack of evidence. They said that they believe neighbors denounced them to the authorities because of their sexual orientation. One of the five, a 23-year-old man, said: We were arrested while preparing for a fashion show at my place. Around 9 p.m., three police officers arrived, took us to the station and confiscated our phones.... We were held for two days, then taken to the This prosecutor's office and charged with acts against nature, despite not being caught in the act.... I think our neighbors told the police we are gay because they were jealous of our successful fashion business. He said that, "we were beaten, whipped, and slapped, and called homosexuals.... I was injured on my thigh, causing lasting pain." A social worker operating in Rebeuss, Senegal's largest detention facility, located in Dakar, said he witnessed prison staff and detainees discriminate against those held on suspicion of homosexuality: "[LGBT detainees] are being excluded from communal activities, denied participation in collective prayer sessions, and required to access services, including the barber, separately from other prisoners. In some cases, they are even compelled to perform domestic labor." Prolonged Pretrial Detention Since February, only one person arrested for "acts against nature" has been convicted according tolocal media. On April 10, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court, in a suburb of Dakar, sentenced a 24-year-old man, who had been arrested a week earlier, to six years in prison and imposed a fine of 2 million CFA franc (approximately $3,300) after convicting him of "acts against nature" and "public indecency." He was not represented by legal counsel as it is often the case for people accused of "acts against nature" who may be denied access to legal representation or face difficulty finding lawyers willing to represent them. A lawyer in Dakar told Human Rights Watch that many of those arrested on homosexuality-related charges remain in pretrial detention because prosecutors have added supplementary charges, including criminal association, endangering the life of others, deliberate HIV transmission, and drug trafficking. The lawyer said that these additional charges often require longer investigations and are used to justify extending pretrial detention. Senegalese law generally limits pretrial detention to six months for minor offenses, with no limit for certain serious crimes such as murder, offenses against state security, and embezzlement of public funds.International human rights law requires that pretrial detention should be an exception, not the rule, and be justified on an individual basis in every case. Anyone held in pretrial detention is entitled to a trial within a reasonable time or release. Lengthy pretrial detention remains a significant concern in Senegal, as several civil society organizations and government officials interviewed said. On August 7, the Pikine-Guediawaye District Court officiallyclosed the preliminary investigation into the case involving the 12 men arrested on February 9 and another 87 people arrested in connection with the same crackdown. The court dismissed cases for 28 and freed them, but 71 remain referred to trial on charges of criminal association and acts against nature. The district court also dismissed charges of "endangering other people's lives" and "voluntary HIV transmission." This decision raises questions regarding continued detention of the 12 accused as the investigative needs that are commonly invoked to justify prolonged pretrial detention may no longer apply. Barriers to Legal Representation Human Rights Watch found that that the newly introduced offense of "promotion of homosexuality" has had a chilling effect on access to legal representation. Lawyers and human rights defenders said they were concerned that representing people charged under article 319 could expose them to professional, social, or even legal repercussions. "How can we represent people arrested without being accused of promotion," one lawyer said. "That's why there is such strong reluctance." The lawyer described serious obstacles to accessing legal representation, saying that detainees, including his own client, were pressured to waive their right to legal representation. He also said that authorities frequently questioned detainees and obtained statements in the absence of legal counsel. On February 9, the lawyer filed two complaints before the Dakar Court of Appeals, one on his own behalf and one on behalf of his client against a gendarmerie commander who pressured his client to waive his right to legal representation. He said in September that no progress had been made in either case. Another lawyer raised concern about gendarmes' respect for due process. He suspected that authorities had obtained his clients "confessions" without their fully understanding of the proceedings and the implications of their statements. Forced HIV Testing; Disclosure of Medical Information RADDHO and HIV Justice Network told Human Rights Watch that the authorities have forced most detainees to undergo HIV testing and, when the results were positive, charged them with "deliberate HIV transmission" and "endangering the lives of others" in addition to offenses under article 319 of the amended penal code. Under article 36 of Senegal's 2010law on HIV/AIDS, anyone who is knowingly living with HIV and has unprotected sex may face 5 to 10 years in prison and a fine. The Keur Massar gendarmerie hasofficially stated that they required arrested people to undergo HIV tests. The national police also have conducted such tests and used the HIV status in criminal proceedings, as they mentioned in their June 13statement. "We are aware about nonconsensual HIV testing by gendarmerie and disclosure of people's HIV status," a doctor told Human Rights Watch. The consequences of these practices have extended beyond individual detainees. Health professionals said that the use of HIV-related services has sharply declined and attribute it to fear of arrest, forced disclosure, and social stigma. "If, because of the law, people decide to stop coming to health clinics, it becomes a public health problem," a doctor said. The Public Health Ministry and the National Council for the Fight Against AIDS (Conseil National de Lutte Contre le Sida, or CNLS), a government body leading and coordinating the HIV response in Senegal, released joint statements on Facebook onFebruary 11 andFebruary 23 stressing national efforts to treat and prevent HIV/AIDS and support people living with HIV/AIDS, as well as the need to keep medical and judicial records separate, and the difficulty of establishing intentional transmission. In a March 18 news statement, the Joint UN Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS), which advocates for global action against the HIV/AIDS pandemic, expressed concerns over the impact of the amended law, andcalled on Senegal to protect the confidentiality of medical information and the patient-provider relationship as non-negotiable foundations of a functioning health system. Breaches of Privacy and Confidentiality Numerous local media reports on the recent cases include highly detailed personal information about individuals arrested by the security forces. In at least four cases, the information closely tracks information in case records, nearly verbatim, suggesting that confidential information was being directly shared with journalists. "Our photos and items found [by Police] at my home, like lubricants and antiretroviral tablets, were published in newspapers and on social media," the 23-year-old man said. In one prominent case, a rare instance in which the detainee had legal representation after his arrest, Keur Massar gendarmes detained a popular artist on charges of "acts against nature," and his name, HIV status, and other confidential information appeared soon afterward in themedia. As a Senegalese journalist put it: "Publishing 'scandalous' information, on such a taboo matter like homosexuality in Senegal, has increasingly become a means of driving audience engagement. This practice turns people's suffering into spectacle, with little regard for the serious consequences for those whose privacy and dignity are violated." Mental Health Consequences of the Crackdown The government crackdown has had serious social and psychological effects on LGBT people across the country. LGBT individuals interviewed said they experienced fear, anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts, and many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements, withdrawn from social and online life, relocated, or abandoned mobile phones to avoid detection by the security forces. A 22-year-old university student said he was forced to move after facing verbal threats and harassment: In the neighborhood where I was, people started insulting me. They would say things like 'next time it is your turn,' when I passed [by them]. Kids would even follow me singing 'goor-jigeen' [a Wolof word describing a man who appears and behaves like a woman] and adults would say nothing. I couldn't even defend myself. I knew if I said something, they would all come after me. To come back home I had to wait until it is dark so no one would notice me. A 27-year-old community worker in Dakar, said constant fear has turned daily life "into a state resembling COVID confinement": We have suspended all our activities, including online. Now nobody trusts anyone. There is a total lack of security. I know I have one foot in prison. I can be arrested anytime because I am a community leader. Even if I am not in prison right now, I live like I am in prison. Life has totally changed. Another 21-year-old man among those arrested in December 2025 said that, following his release in January 2026, he has been living in hiding in central Senegal, unable to return home out of fear his relatives would assault him: I received a call from my mother telling me not to come back home. articles.title: Senegal: Brutal Crackdown Violates LGBT People
